question: When US towns switched telephone exchanges to automatic dialling, cutting operator jobs, what happened to employment among the next generation of young women?
options: It held, as they found other work
It fell with the lost operator jobs
answer: It held. Economists comparing cities switched at different times between 1920 and 1940 found cutovers cut young women's operator jobs by 50 to 80%, yet later cohorts were no less likely to work: they moved into clerical and service jobs. The cost fell on operators already in post, more of whom ended in worse-paid work.
move: Count what people did next, not only the jobs that vanished.
trap: It fell, since every lost operator job looks like a lost worker.
source: Feigenbaum & Gross, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2024
reference: Feigenbaum & Gross, Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2024
